sections.title: Quick answer

body: Both labels share the four letters within NERIS. To interpret a report, use the definitions from the assessment that produced it.
Identity describes how people evaluate themselves and respond to pressure. It cannot establish how accurate someone’s judgment was.
The Myers–Briggs convention used here puts Ne first, Fi second, Te third and Si fourth. The Foundation also allows Ti for tertiary Thinking. NERIS does not use Jungian function stacks.

If two results differ, check whether they use the same instrument and language. If both provide comparable scores and explain the cutoff, check how close the scores are. The change in label alone cannot establish why it happened.
### Why the two ends have to be compared inside the same event
Compare the same feedback, information, responsibilities and time. Differences in circumstances can affect both the decision and how it feels.

In a fictional community event, two organisers hear that a section felt scattered. Both ask which section and check the same outline. One may still feel confident in the rest of the session. The other may feel less sure about it.

If only one person can approve a change, their different responses may reflect their roles. Read the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) for the four letters and the [NERIS framework](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) for Identity.
sections.title: ENFP-A and ENFP-T: what they share and where they part

body: Each fictional row holds the information, responsibilities and deadline constant.
The A and T columns compare possible self-evaluations. Either person can take the actions in the fourth column.

| Shared situation | Assertive (A): possible self-evaluation | Turbulent (T): possible self-evaluation | What either person can do | Aspect of Identity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both hear that the opening has too many activities | May still feel confident in the rest of the plan | May also feel less sure about the rest of the plan | Ask which activity caused confusion | Self-evaluation |
| Both hear the same objections from two collaborators | May retain confidence in their initial judgment | May feel less sure about their initial judgment | Agree on the evidence that would justify a revision | Self-assurance |
| Both complete the same week of revisions | May still feel confident about the plan | May feel less certain that the plan will work | Agree what still needs checking and what counts as done | Response to pressure |
| Both explain the same next step | May feel confident they considered the concerns | May worry that they overlooked a concern | Ask whether anything remains unclear | Self-assurance |
| Both sign off after completing the same form checks | May still feel sure about their review | May feel less sure they caught every issue | Record the checks and who approved the form | Self-assurance under responsibility |
| Both receive the same compliment after the event | May feel confident that their work went well | May still feel unsure about how they did | Ask which part worked well | Self-evaluation |
Both organisers should check a possible factual error or safety issue through the same process. How sure they feel does not change that requirement.
sections.title: ENFP-A and ENFP-T in one minute

body: The four fictional scenes follow one community session. In each, both organisers have the same feedback, decision rights and remaining time.
### ENFP-A and ENFP-T deciding whether to change the opening
(Fictional example) A participant says newcomers cannot tell which opening activity comes first. Both organisers hear the same comment and review the same sign-in instructions.

Both organisers revise the same unclear step. After making the change, one might feel confident in the rest of the opening, while the other might feel less sure about how well they planned it. The revision itself says nothing about A/T.
Ask a willing first-time participant to try the revised instructions. If they cannot locate the check-in point, ask where they got stuck before deciding what to change.
### ENFP-A and ENFP-T responding to a volunteer's point
(Fictional example) A volunteer says only two people may arrive early. Both organisers have the same schedule and authority to adjust coverage.
Both confirm the same staffing gap and agree on the same change. One might still feel sure about the rest of the schedule, while the other might question whether they missed something elsewhere.
Assign duties by availability and venue knowledge. Check that the revised plan covers the entrance and check-in.
### ENFP-A and ENFP-T renegotiating the division with a friend
(Fictional example) A friend says they do not want to announce the whole session. Both organisers hear the same request.

Both ask what the friend is willing to do and revise the assignment with their agreement. One may see the change as a routine adjustment, while the other may feel less sure about their judgment in assigning roles.
Ask whether the friend would prefer a smaller role or to step out of that part altogether. Confirm who takes over before publishing the new plan.
### ENFP-A and ENFP-T ending the checking when pressure rises
(Fictional example) Several practice runs stall at the same instruction. Both organisers use the same criteria to decide when the instructions are ready.

Ask a first-time participant to follow the revised instructions. If the agreed check passes, both organisers can stop revising. One may still feel less confident about the event as a whole. That feeling does not change the check or determine the suffix.
For each problem, record what the organisers knew, what they changed and how they felt about their judgment. Those are three separate questions.
sections.title: ENFP-A and ENFP-T in work and relationships

body: A/T describes self-assurance and responses to pressure within NERIS. It cannot establish resilience, sensitivity in every situation or judgment accuracy.
Someone may reply quickly because they are keeping time. Another may wait until a volunteer confirms. Neither response identifies an A/T result.
The official MBTI code is ENFP. F is the third letter and stands for Feeling. A or T after a hyphen describes NERIS Identity. Similar codes do not make the instruments equivalent.
A single performance cannot establish either end. Checking work or changing your mind can happen at either end.
### Which statements cannot be used to type anyone
The suffix cannot rank people by maturity, mental health or work ability.
Look at the relevant facts when you evaluate a decision. Someone can feel uncertain after a good decision or sure of one that needs to change.
sections.title: ENFP-A and ENFP-T: avoiding misreads

body: Use this exercise to reflect on how a situation felt. It cannot produce an Identity result or assess career fit.
Write down the feedback, what it showed and how confident you felt. The same person can react differently to similar feedback on another day.

After feedback, describe how certain you felt and how much pressure you felt. Revisit both notes after clarification. There is no score or cutoff to apply. Stop if recording makes you dwell on it or interferes with sleep or work. If distress persists, consider seeking qualified support.
When comparing reports, use the same instrument and language under similar conditions. If scores and scoring notes are available, check the cutoff. A label change alone does not establish its cause.
### Conditions easily overlooked when observing
Compare situations with similar responsibility, time and familiarity.
Record who could approve a change, the time available and what each person knew. If those conditions differ, they can affect how people act and feel.

body: **Framework sources.** The definitions of the two ends follow the [NERIS explanation from 16Personalities](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) and the [dedicated Identity page](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent); the four-letter part refers to the preference and process framework set out in the [Foundation's type dynamics table](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Function-stack convention.** This page uses Ne–Fi–Te–Si for ENFP in Myers–Briggs type dynamics. The Foundation also allows Ti for tertiary Thinking. NERIS does not use a function stack. The suffix cannot predict behaviour or ability.
**Editorial fiction.** The event, schedule, division of work, sign-up exercise and observation examples are fictional. They do not establish how often a reaction occurs or measure any individual.

**Scope.** NERIS defines the A/T suffixes. FermatMind uses its own items and scoring. Do not use the suffix to screen job applicants, rank ability or predict relationships. See the [method and evidence statement](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

faq.answer:
The official MBTI uses the four-letter code ENFP. The A and T suffixes belong to the separate NERIS model.

faq.answer:

body: ENFP-A and ENFP-T share the ENFP code. In 16Personalities’ NERIS model, Assertive (A) describes greater self-assurance and less sensitivity to stress, while Turbulent (T) describes more self-doubt and greater sensitivity to stress.
The Myers–Briggs code stands for Extraversion, Intuition, Feeling and Perceiving. Its type-dynamics convention used here is Ne–Fi–Te–Si. NERIS uses a similar code and its own scales.
The A and T suffixes mark opposite ends of NERIS Identity. The official MBTI uses four letters. The T after the hyphen means Turbulent, separate from Thinking in an MBTI code.

Two organisers can hear the same criticism, check the same opening activity and make the same revision. Afterwards, they may feel differently about how well they did. The fictional example illustrates a difference in self-evaluation without assigning the action to either end.
sections.title: Quick answer

body: Both labels share the four letters within NERIS. To interpret a report, use the definitions from the assessment that produced it.
Identity describes how people evaluate themselves and respond to pressure. It cannot establish how accurate someone’s judgment was.
The Myers–Briggs convention used here puts Ne first, Fi second, Te third and Si fourth. The Foundation also allows Ti for tertiary Thinking. NERIS does not use Jungian function stacks.

If two results differ, check whether they use the same instrument and language. If both provide comparable scores and explain the cutoff, check how close the scores are. The change in label alone cannot establish why it happened.
### Why the two ends have to be compared inside the same event
Compare the same feedback, information, responsibilities and time. Differences in circumstances can affect both the decision and how it feels.

In a fictional community event, two organisers hear that a section felt scattered. Both ask which section and check the same outline. One may still feel confident in the rest of the session. The other may feel less sure about it.

If only one person can approve a change, their different responses may reflect their roles. Read the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) for the four letters and the [NERIS framework](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) for Identity.

body: Each fictional row holds the information, responsibilities and deadline constant.
The A and T columns compare possible self-evaluations. Either person can take the actions in the fourth column.

| Shared situation | Assertive (A): possible self-evaluation | Turbulent (T): possible self-evaluation | What either person can do | Aspect of Identity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both hear that the opening has too many activities | May still feel confident in the rest of the plan | May also feel less sure about the rest of the plan | Ask which activity caused confusion | Self-evaluation |
| Both hear the same objections from two collaborators | May retain confidence in their initial judgment | May feel less sure about their initial judgment | Agree on the evidence that would justify a revision | Self-assurance |
| Both complete the same week of revisions | May still feel confident about the plan | May feel less certain that the plan will work | Agree what still needs checking and what counts as done | Response to pressure |
| Both explain the same next step | May feel confident they considered the concerns | May worry that they overlooked a concern | Ask whether anything remains unclear | Self-assurance |
| Both sign off after completing the same form checks | May still feel sure about their review | May feel less sure they caught every issue | Record the checks and who approved the form | Self-assurance under responsibility |
| Both receive the same compliment after the event | May feel confident that their work went well | May still feel unsure about how they did | Ask which part worked well | Self-evaluation |
Both organisers should check a possible factual error or safety issue through the same process. How sure they feel does not change that requirement.

body: The four fictional scenes follow one community session. In each, both organisers have the same feedback, decision rights and remaining time.
### ENFP-A and ENFP-T deciding whether to change the opening
(Fictional example) A participant says newcomers cannot tell which opening activity comes first. Both organisers hear the same comment and review the same sign-in instructions.

Both organisers revise the same unclear step. After making the change, one might feel confident in the rest of the opening, while the other might feel less sure about how well they planned it. The revision itself says nothing about A/T.
Ask a willing first-time participant to try the revised instructions. If they cannot locate the check-in point, ask where they got stuck before deciding what to change.
### ENFP-A and ENFP-T responding to a volunteer's point
(Fictional example) A volunteer says only two people may arrive early. Both organisers have the same schedule and authority to adjust coverage.
Both confirm the same staffing gap and agree on the same change. One might still feel sure about the rest of the schedule, while the other might question whether they missed something elsewhere.
Assign duties by availability and venue knowledge. Check that the revised plan covers the entrance and check-in.
### ENFP-A and ENFP-T renegotiating the division with a friend
(Fictional example) A friend says they do not want to announce the whole session. Both organisers hear the same request.

Both ask what the friend is willing to do and revise the assignment with their agreement. One may see the change as a routine adjustment, while the other may feel less sure about their judgment in assigning roles.
Ask whether the friend would prefer a smaller role or to step out of that part altogether. Confirm who takes over before publishing the new plan.
### ENFP-A and ENFP-T ending the checking when pressure rises
(Fictional example) Several practice runs stall at the same instruction. Both organisers use the same criteria to decide when the instructions are ready.

Ask a first-time participant to follow the revised instructions. If the agreed check passes, both organisers can stop revising. One may still feel less confident about the event as a whole. That feeling does not change the check or determine the suffix.
For each problem, record what the organisers knew, what they changed and how they felt about their judgment. Those are three separate questions.

body: A/T describes self-assurance and responses to pressure within NERIS. It cannot establish resilience, sensitivity in every situation or judgment accuracy.
Someone may reply quickly because they are keeping time. Another may wait until a volunteer confirms. Neither response identifies an A/T result.
The official MBTI code is ENFP. F is the third letter and stands for Feeling. A or T after a hyphen describes NERIS Identity. Similar codes do not make the instruments equivalent.
A single performance cannot establish either end. Checking work or changing your mind can happen at either end.
### Which statements cannot be used to type anyone
The suffix cannot rank people by maturity, mental health or work ability.
Look at the relevant facts when you evaluate a decision. Someone can feel uncertain after a good decision or sure of one that needs to change.
sections.title: ENFP-A and ENFP-T: avoiding misreads

body: Use this exercise to reflect on how a situation felt. It cannot produce an Identity result or assess career fit.
Write down the feedback, what it showed and how confident you felt. The same person can react differently to similar feedback on another day.

After feedback, describe how certain you felt and how much pressure you felt. Revisit both notes after clarification. There is no score or cutoff to apply. Stop if recording makes you dwell on it or interferes with sleep or work. If distress persists, consider seeking qualified support.
When comparing reports, use the same instrument and language under similar conditions. If scores and scoring notes are available, check the cutoff. A label change alone does not establish its cause.
### Conditions easily overlooked when observing
Compare situations with similar responsibility, time and familiarity.
Record who could approve a change, the time available and what each person knew. If those conditions differ, they can affect how people act and feel.

body: **Framework sources.** The definitions of the two ends follow the [NERIS explanation from 16Personalities](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) and the [dedicated Identity page](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent); the four-letter part refers to the preference and process framework set out in the [Foundation's type dynamics table](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Function-stack convention.** This page uses Ne–Fi–Te–Si for ENFP in Myers–Briggs type dynamics. The Foundation also allows Ti for tertiary Thinking. NERIS does not use a function stack. The suffix cannot predict behaviour or ability.
**Editorial fiction.** The event, schedule, division of work, sign-up exercise and observation examples are fictional. They do not establish how often a reaction occurs or measure any individual.

**Scope.** NERIS defines the A/T suffixes. FermatMind uses its own items and scoring. Do not use the suffix to screen job applicants, rank ability or predict relationships. See the [method and evidence statement](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

**Framework sources.** The definitions of the two ends follow the [NERIS explanation from 16Personalities](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) and the [dedicated Identity page](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent); the four-letter part refers to the preference and process framework set out in the [Foundation's type dynamics table](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Function-stack convention.** This page uses Ne–Fi–Te–Si for ENFP in Myers–Briggs type dynamics. The Foundation also allows Ti for tertiary Thinking. NERIS does not use a function stack. The suffix cannot predict behaviour or ability.

**Editorial fiction.** The event, schedule, division of work, sign-up exercise and observation examples are fictional. They do not establish how often a reaction occurs or measure any individual.

**Scope.** NERIS defines the A/T suffixes. FermatMind uses its own items and scoring. Do not use the suffix to screen job applicants, rank ability or predict relationships. See the [method and evidence statement](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
